paragraph.text: N6. "Meddling with nature is wrong; we could make everything worse"

the risk of making things worse is real, and that's exactly why the serious proposal isn't to start intervening, but to study first: this is what's called welfare biology. Medicine can also make things worse, and the response was to create research, trials and caution, not to abandon the sick. Besides, we already meddle with nature all the time, for ourselves; what's missing is taking into account the animals that live in it.
N. Wild animals, new minds and the future ·
DIR

this family takes the sentience criterion beyond exploitation. Many vegans disagree with parts of it, and the debate is legitimate. The test proposed in each chapter is simple: apply the same scenario to human beings and see whether the answer would be accepted; if it would not, that shows speciesism.
1. Formulation
"Every time humans meddle with nature, it goes wrong. Let nature take care of itself."
Ecosystems are complex systems, with knock-on effects that are hard to predict.
Human interventions in ecosystems have already caused disasters, such as introducing species that became pests.
An intervention to reduce suffering could end up increasing it.
So we shouldn't intervene in nature to help animals.
P1, P2 and P3 are true and need to be taken seriously. The problem is the conclusion: from the risk of getting it wrong, what follows isn't a ban on acting, but a requirement to act with knowledge.
The argument is
: the correct conclusion from the premises is "we shouldn't intervene without study", not "we should never intervene".
2. How it can show up
Context
Typical form

3. Answer for children

When a doctor isn't sure which medicine will work, they don't leave the person untreated: they study, run tests and try carefully. It's the same with animals in nature. Scientists need to study a lot before helping, so as not to make things worse. But studying is already a way to start helping.
4. Short answer

The risk of making things worse is real. That's why no serious person proposes meddling with ecosystems at random: they propose studying first, testing on a small scale, and only expanding what works. It's what medicine does with risky treatments. And we already meddle with nature all the time for ourselves; the question is whether the animals living in it count too.
"Since treatments can go wrong, should we close the hospitals, or should we research so we get it wrong less often?"
5. Full answer
(a) Reconstruction and diagnosis
The argument starts from a truth and draws too big a conclusion from it:
What is true
What doesn't follow
Poorly planned interventions can make everything worse
Every intervention will make everything worse
Ecosystems are complex
The complexity can never be studied
We should be cautious
We should stand still forever
The proposal of
, suggested by the economist Yew-Kwang Ng in 1995, is precisely to answer risk with knowledge: studying the wellbeing of wild animals and the effects of interventions before scaling them up.
(b) Where the argument breaks

text.bold: 1. Risk calls for study, not omission.

paragraph.text: In every field where acting is risky, such as medicine, engineering or public policy, the response was to create methods for getting it wrong less: research, trials, small and reversible interventions.

text.bold: 2. We already meddle with nature, a lot.

paragraph.text: About half of the planet's habitable land is used for agriculture. We dam rivers, build cities, plant forests, reintroduce and eliminate species. We do this for human interests or environmental goals. What rarely enters the calculation is the wellbeing of the animals affected.
Omission isn't neutral: it lets existing suffering continue. Comparing "intervening" with "doing nothing" as if the second option had no cost is an accounting error.

When a human population faces an epidemic, we know interventions can have unexpected effects. The response is to study and act carefully, not to let the epidemic run its course because "meddling makes it worse". Applying the rule of omission only to animals is deciding by species.

text.bold: 5. Some kinds of help have low risk and known effects.

paragraph.text: Rescuing animals in floods, treating the injured and vaccinating against specific diseases are limited, studied interventions that are already practised.

text.bold: 6. The objection only appears when the beneficiary is the animal.

paragraph.text: Grace Clement (2003), Jennifer Everett (2001) and Aaron Simmons (2009) argue that ecosystems are too complex to intervene in for the animals' good. But equally complex ecosystems are intervened in every day for human and environmental goals, and no one forbids it on those grounds. Using risk as a veto only when the one who benefits is the wild animal is a double standard (Cunha, 2022, p. 243).

If we can't predict the effect of intervening, we can't know that not intervening is better either (Cowen, 2003; Torres Aldave, 2015). And the choice isn't between knowing everything and knowing nothing: we work with probabilities, as in any decision. No one refuses to help a person stand up because they don't know what that person will do next (Cunha, 2022, pp. 243–244).

text.bold: 8. The harm of omission almost never enters the calculation.

paragraph.text: Any harm an intervention might cause is used to condemn it, but the certain and enormous harm of leaving everything as it is is rarely weighed. Comparing the risk of helping with a cost-free "nothing" is the same mistake as in point 3, on a much larger scale (Cunha, 2022, pp. 246–247).

text.bold: 9. "We don't know what's good for them" proves too much.

paragraph.text: If we knew nothing about animals' good, we couldn't know that leaving them as they are is best either. Those who raise this objection usually claim, rightly, that factory farms harm animals; if we know when the harm comes from humans, we know when it comes from nature. Not knowing everything isn't knowing nothing: every sentient animal avoids burns, drowning, hunger and being eaten alive. And ignorance, where it exists, calls for research, not abstention (Cunha, 2022, pp. 139–141).

It's said that saving a wild animal only postpones a worse death. But in most cases, what makes the animal suffer is the same thing that kills it, hunger or disease; saving it removes the source of suffering. Animals with few young, such as elephants or deer, can have good lives with water, food, vaccines and treatment. And some help prolongs no life at all: it only prevents the birth of young destined to die soon (Cunha, 2022, pp. 259–261; Faria, 2016; N23).

Holmes Rolston III (1992) and the veterinarians James Kirkwood and Anthony Sainsbury (1996) argue that helping the less fit harms the species. But the species feels nothing; individuals do. A trait only spreads after generations of individuals without it dying young. There are other ways out, such as reducing reproduction. And, applied to humans, the idea would be a "natural" eugenics: refusing vaccines and medicines to the sick to strengthen the population (Cunha, 2022, pp. 254–256; N24).

text.bold: 12. "It went wrong before" doesn't describe the past.

paragraph.text: Peter Singer used this objection in

, recalling disastrous interventions in ecosystems. According to Cunha (2022, p. 258, n. 141), Singer revised that position in a 2016 talk on wild animal suffering, in which he came to treat the issue as important and to argue for research. And the interventions that went wrong had human or environmental goals; there has never been a large-scale attempt to reduce wild animal suffering. What was learned from them increases, rather than decreases, our ability to predict (Cunha, 2022, pp. 258–259).

Cunha (2022, pp. 257–258, 261–262) proposes rules that answer most of the fear of making things worse: no legitimate intervention involves killing animals; outside emergencies, only qualified professionals intervene; nothing large-scale before there are studies; continue the small interventions that have already worked; and decide by the expected impact of each option, that is, the severity of each outcome multiplied by its probability, and not only by the worst imaginable scenario. The ordinary citizen's task is more modest: bring the issue into public debate, support research, and demand that animals' wellbeing count in public decisions.

(d) The strongest counter-reply: we'll never know enough
The most serious version says: ecosystems are so complex that we'll never have enough knowledge to predict the consequences. Humility calls for not intervening.
(e) Why the counter-reply doesn't reach the conclusion

text.bold: Never knowing everything isn't the same as never knowing anything.

paragraph.text: In medicine and ecology we act on partial knowledge all the time, and knowledge grows precisely through research and controlled experience.
We also don't know whether omission is the best option. Assuming not acting is always safe is a form of overconfidence.
Starting with what is local, reversible and observable lets us learn without gambling whole ecosystems.

11. What the argument gets right
It gets a lot right: ecosystems are complex, interventions have caused disasters, and anyone who wants to help wild animals needs humility and method. Grand, hasty proposals would be irresponsible.
But risk is a reason to study, not to give up. And if we accept meddling with nature for so many human reasons, there's no reason to exclude precisely the good of the animals that live in it.
